pharm: Inhibits insulin release from the pancreas to raise blood glucose; also relaxes vascular smooth muscle (vasodilator) and has an antidiuretic, sodium- and water-retaining action
quick: Oral 3 mg/kg/day in 2-3 divided doses, titrated up to 8 mg/kg/day
May be taken with or without food; give consistently
Use only if clearly needed; crosses placenta - neonatal hyperglycaemia, alopecia, hypertrichosis
Caution - excretion into milk not well characterised; weigh benefit/risk
Half-life prolonged - reduce dose and monitor electrolytes
Use cautiously; highly protein-bound, hepatically influenced disposition
Blood glucose, urine glucose/ketones, fluid status, electrolytes, uric acid, CBC
summary: Oral diazoxide (Proglycem) is a non-diuretic benzothiadiazine indicated for the management of hypoglycaemia due to hyperinsulinism - in adults from inoperable islet-cell adenoma/carcinoma or extrapancreatic malignancy, and in infants and children from leucine sensitivity, islet-cell hyperplasia, nesidioblastosis, islet-cell adenoma/adenomatosis or extrapancreatic malignancy - and may be used peri-operatively. It raises blood glucose mainly by opening pancreatic ATP-sensitive potassium channels and inhibiting insulin secretion, with onset within an hour and a duration usually under 8 hours in normal renal function. The recommended adult/child starting dose is 3 mg/kg/day in 2-3 divided doses, titrated to a maximum of 8 mg/kg/day; infants and newborns start at 8 mg/kg/day up to 15 mg/kg/day. Key hazards are HYPERGLYCAEMIA progressing to diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma, and significant sodium and FLUID RETENTION that can precipitate heart failure; pulmonary hypertension has been reported in neonates and infants. (Parenteral diazoxide was historically used for hypertensive emergencies.)
indications: Management of hypoglycaemia due to hyperinsulinism in adults - inoperable islet-cell adenoma or carcinoma, or extrapancreatic malignancy

Management of hypoglycaemia due to hyperinsulinism in infants and children - leucine sensitivity, islet-cell hyperplasia, nesidioblastosis, extrapancreatic malignancy, islet-cell adenoma or adenomatosis
Pre-operative temporary control and post-operative control of persistent hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
Historical/parenteral: hypertensive emergency (IV diazoxide, now rarely used)

Take special care with dosing accuracy in infants and young children

moa: Diazoxide is a benzothiadiazine that, unlike thiazide diuretics, does not increase sodium excretion. It produces a dose-related rise in blood glucose primarily by opening ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells, hyperpolarising the membrane and inhibiting insulin release, with an additional extrapancreatic effect. It relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, giving a vasodilator/antihypertensive action when given intravenously. It also exerts an antidiuretic effect, decreasing sodium and water excretion and causing fluid retention, and raises serum uric acid by reducing its renal excretion. Its hyperglycaemic effect begins within about an hour and lasts up to 8 hours with normal renal function.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to diazoxide, other thiazides, or any excipient
relative: Compromised cardiac reserve / heart failure (fluid retention risk)
Neonates/infants with risk factors for pulmonary hypertension
monitor: Fluid balance, weight and signs of heart failure

preg: Diazoxide crosses the placenta. Reproduction data are limited; adverse effects reported in neonates exposed in utero include hyperglycaemia, alopecia and hypertrichosis lanuginosa, and it can cause fetal/neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, thrombocytopenia and altered carbohydrate metabolism. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed, and monitor exposed infants.
lact: Data on diazoxide in human milk are limited. Caution is advised when treating a nursing mother; weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against potential infant risk and monitor the infant.
renal: Diazoxide is extensively protein-bound and renally excreted, and its plasma half-life (about 28-30 hours) is further prolonged in renal impairment, increasing the risk of accumulation and toxicity. Reduce the dose and monitor serum electrolytes and glucose closely.
hepatic: Diazoxide is highly protein-bound; use cautiously in hepatic impairment and monitor for exaggerated or prolonged effects. Its protein binding can displace bilirubin and warfarin.

major: Phenytoin (diphenylhydantoin) - may cause loss of seizure control; diazoxide can lower phenytoin levels
Insulin / sulfonylureas - antagonised by the hyperglycaemic action of diazoxide
moderate: Thiazide and other diuretics - potentiate the hyperglycaemic and hyperuricaemic effects of diazoxide
Warfarin and coumarin anticoagulants - displaced from protein binding; may need anticoagulant dose reduction
Alpha-adrenergic blockers - antagonise the insulin-release inhibition
minor: Drugs highly bound to albumin may be displaced (e.g. bilirubin in neonates)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; give consistently
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; avoid excessive intake
interactions.diagnostics: Raises blood/urine glucose and serum uric acid; may transiently affect platelet and neutrophil counts

common: Sodium and fluid retention (oedema), most marked in infants and adults
Hirsutism of lanugo type (forehead, back, limbs), especially in children and women - reversible on stopping
Gastrointestinal upset - anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
Tachycardia and palpitations; raised serum uric acid
serious: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma (can develop rapidly)
Congestive heart failure precipitated by fluid retention in compromised hearts
Pulmonary hypertension in neonates and young infants
rare: Transient cataracts in association with hyperosmolar coma
Abnormal facial features with prolonged childhood use
emergency: Diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma
Acute congestive heart failure / pulmonary oedema
Pulmonary hypertension with respiratory distress in infants

monitoring: Blood glucose frequently during initiation and titration
Urine glucose and ketones during prolonged therapy, especially in stress/illness
Fluid balance, body weight and cardiac status
Infants for signs of pulmonary hypertension (respiratory distress)
counsel: This medicine raises blood sugar to treat dangerously low glucose from too much insulin
Watch for swelling of the ankles, sudden weight gain or breathlessness and report them promptly
Test urine for sugar and ketones as advised, and report excessive thirst, frequent urination or vomiting
Increased fine body or facial hair can occur, especially in children and women, and reverses after stopping
Do not stop the medicine suddenly - low blood sugar can return; keep all monitoring appointments
Because the drug stays in the body a long time, effects of an overdose can last up to a week
pk: Hyperglycaemic effect begins within about 1 hour of an oral dose
Variable; effect generally established within hours
About 28-36 hours (approximately 30 h); 9.5-24 h in some children; prolonged in renal impairment
Hyperglycaemic effect usually lasts up to 8 hours with normal renal function
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from light; protect oral suspension from light
pearls: Opposite of an antidiabetic: diazoxide RAISES blood glucose by inhibiting insulin release - used for hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
Causes significant sodium/fluid retention - can precipitate heart failure and is often combined with a diuretic
Hyperglycaemia can progress to ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar coma; monitor glucose and ketones
Pulmonary hypertension reported in neonates/infants - watch for respiratory distress and stop if suspected
Long half-life (~30 h) means overdose effects persist for up to 7 days and require prolonged surveillance
Hirsutism (lanugo) is common and reversible; potentiated hyperglycaemia/hyperuricaemia with thiazides
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not take a double dose. Check your blood sugar if you are unsure, and contact your healthcare team if you miss several doses.
overdose: Overdose causes marked hyperglycaemia that may be associated with ketoacidosis. There is no specific antidote. Because of the long half-life (about 30 hours), monitor blood glucose and ketones for up to 7 days until levels stabilise. Treat hyperglycaemia with insulin and restore fluid and electrolyte balance; haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis can lower drug levels.
